newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch offshore supplier IHC Caland posts higher 1996 profit.
newsitem.headline: Dutch offshore supplier IHC Caland posts higher 1996 profit.

text.p: Dutch shipbuilding and engineering group IHC Caland NV said on Tuesday that preliminary 1996 net profit rose 23.5 percent to 93 million guilders ($50 million) and earnings were set to grow a further 18 percent in 1997.

"Based on the current order portfolio and the outlook on the promising markets in which the group is active, management expects that net group profits will rise by some 18 percent to some 110 million guilders in 1997," IHC Caland said.
The firm, a supplier of material for the offshore oilfield services, dredging and shipping industries, is widely watched by analysts looking for pointers to future industry performance.
The company, which posted 1995 full-year net of 75.3 million guilders, had been expected by analysts to post a 1996 net profit of between 91.8 and 99 million guilders.
Earnings per share growth was braked by a 2.4 million increase in shares outstanding following last June's private share placement.
Preliminary net profit per share rose 16.4 percent to 3.69 guilders from a year-earlier 3.17 guilders. In 1997, earnings per share are seen rising 12 percent.
On the Amsterdam Stock Exchange, IHC shares fell to a low of 106.50 guilders from 113.40 guilders at the open before recovering slightly to 108.60 guilders.
Dealers said the share price fall reflected investor disappointment at the forecast slowdown in 1997 earnings growth.

IHC said all its units had positively contributed to the 1996 results. It had delivered orders totalling 1.512 billion guilders compared with 928 million in 1995 but added its gross profit margin had deteriorated in 1996 as predicted.
The company won new orders totalling 1.610 billion guilders, down from 1.861 billion in 1995.
By the end of 1996, IHC Caland's order book had grown to 3.043 billion guilders, up from 2.962 billion one year earlier.
IHC said these new orders confirmed management optimism about the markets in which it was active.
The major international oil companies were set to increase exploration and production budgets by some 15 percent in 1997, IHC Caland said, with the lion's share going to offshore activities.
IHC's order book includes seven long-term contracts with oil companies for floating production and storage units.
"This will secure a considerable stream of revenues for many years to come, which in turn will enable the group to invest further in new lease projects," IHC said.
